WASHINGTON — U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks (both D-Md.) and Senator Cory Booker (D-N.J.), along with five of their colleagues representing the Mid-Atlantic region, are pushing for emergency agricultural disaster funding to support farmers in their states who have been impacted by the April 2026 regional freeze event. The lawmakers' letter to the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies stresses the need to provide relief to farmers facing losses from the April 2026 freeze and frost event that destroyed crops in the region. Senators Van Hollen, Alsobrooks, and Booker were joined in sending this letter by Senators Mark Warner (D-Va.), Kristen Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), and Andy Kim (D-N.J.). On the devastating impact of the April freeze, the Senators wrote , “In the early morning hours of April 21, 2026, the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States experienced a severe temperature drop, resulting in a freeze that devastated specialty crops across seven states including Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Delaware, New York, New Jersey, and West Virginia. This region, which is among the top areas of the country for specialty crop production, experienced devastating and historic losses, including hundreds of millions of dollars in damage with some farmers and companies experiencing complete loss of their crop. In addition to crop loss, some growers are facing permanent damage to their trees and grapevines compounded by ongoing drought conditions throughout the region which will have lasting implications beyond this season.” The Senators continued , “The most recent survey in Maryland puts value-added losses from grape crop damage alone at $30.4 million, with a preliminary survey from the Maryland Farm Bureau indicating that almost all impacted growers sustained major losses, with the average estimated crop loss at 67.5% and the hardest hit areas facing near-total losses of 90% or higher across surveyed crops. In New Jersey, preliminary estimates point to at least $135-$170 million in damage from the freeze, with significant additional losses expected to be reported in the coming months... Producers across the Mid-Atlantic continue to face the challenges of labor and maintenance for their farms, despite the absence of a harvestable crop to offset the costs. This has resulted in significant economic hardship for the industry.” “Congress has consistently demonstrated support of specialty crop growers through policy and appropriations. While this freeze event has informed meaningful conversations on improving existing emergency relief programs long-term, the urgency of the immediate need for relief for specialty crop producers in the Mid-Atlantic cannot wait. We appreciate your support for specialty crops in the Mid-Atlantic and look forward to your partnership in providing critical relief for producers,” the Senators concluded . This letter builds on the successful effort Senators Van Hollen and Alsobrooks led to ensure the United States Department of Agriculture approved the State of Maryland’s request for an agricultural disaster declaration following the April freeze to make emergency financial assistance programs available to impacted Maryland farmers as quickly as possible. The full text of the letter is available here and below. Dear Chairman Hoeven and Ranking Member Shaheen: As Senators representing states impacted by the devastating freeze event in April 2026 in the Mid-Atlantic region, we respectfully submit an appropriations request for emergency agricultural disaster funding as part of a supplemental funding bill this year to provide relief to farmers facing losses from the recent freeze. In the early morning hours of April 21, 2026, the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States experienced a severe temperature drop, resulting in a freeze that devastated specialty crops across seven states including Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Delaware, New York, New Jersey, and West Virginia. This region, which is among the top areas of the country for specialty crop production, experienced devastating and historic losses, including hundreds of millions of dollars in damage with some farmers and companies experiencing complete loss of their crop. In addition to crop loss, some growers are facing permanent damage to their trees and grapevines compounded by ongoing drought conditions throughout the region which will have lasting implications beyond this season. For example, preliminary estimates from Pennsylvania’s Department of Agriculture indicate that specialty crop farmers are facing $150-$200 million in damages from the freeze. The most recent survey in Maryland puts value-added losses from grape crop damage alone at $30.4 million, with a preliminary survey from the Maryland Farm Bureau indicating that almost all impacted growers sustained major losses, with the average estimated crop loss at 67.5% and the hardest hit areas facing near-total losses of 90% or higher across surveyed crops. And in New Jersey, preliminary estimates point to at least $135-$170 million of damage from the freeze, with significant additional losses expected to be reported in the coming months. Producers across the Mid-Atlantic continue to face the challenges of labor and maintenance for their farms, despite the absence of a harvestable crop to offset the costs. This has resulted in significant economic hardship for the industry. Further exacerbating the challenges are the gaps in specialty crop qualification for key Federal emergency relief programs. While USDA continues to work towards a long-term solution to improve these programs for specialty crop farmers, Mid-Atlantic farmers facing losses from the freeze need immediate relief. It is imperative that Congress provide emergency funding for impacted Mid-Atlantic farmers as soon as possible, and that the funding be accessible to specialty crop farmers and made available to adequately address the range of losses they are experiencing as a result of the freeze. Congress has consistently demonstrated support of specialty crop growers through policy and appropriations. While this freeze event has informed meaningful conversations on improving existing emergency relief programs long-term, the urgency of the immediate need for relief for specialty crop producers in the Mid-Atlantic cannot wait. We appreciate your support for specialty crops in the Mid-Atlantic and look forward to your partnership in providing critical relief for producers. ###

NASA scientists based in Maryland have been key partners in missions like the Hubble, James Webb, and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescopes and the Artemis II mission that sent four astronauts around the Moon for the first time since the 1970s. Our robust industry of large, medium, and small businesses tie the essential private and public partnerships that power economic development and adoption of cutting-edge technology together. After full consideration of all that our state has to offer, we believe it will be clear that Maryland is the natural host for this new institution that will foster the next generation of American space leadership.” They also highlighted the significant concentration of high-quality academic facilities in Maryland that would provide important partnerships for the Space Academy, writing, “Maryland also boasts a world-class network of academic institutions that the Space Academy could draw from. University of Maryland College Park is a top public university renowned for physics, astronomy, and engineering programs and is positioned to provide support to the future Space Academy. Johns Hopkins University, which hosts STScI on its Baltimore campus, leads prominent astrophysics and planetary science research. These industry leaders are building spacecraft and satellites and developing new technology from instruments, to coatings, to flight systems, to everything in between. For the Space Academy students who want to become pilots on their personal journey to reaching space, they can follow in the footsteps of the over eighty astronauts that have trained at the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School at Naval Air Station Patuxent River. That connection also highlights Maryland’s ideal position to help with the continued expansion of the U.S. Space Force. Maryland hosts training facilities for Guardians at Fort Detrick and Joint Base Andrews, as well as many other facilities that support military research and development in other branches, like Fort Meade and Aberdeen Proving Ground. ” “The Space Academy should be located in a state that can maximize opportunities for its students, as the success of the Academy will depend on an unprecedented blend of leadership from academia, civil and commercial space, and the U.S. military. Maryland offers an extensive network of scientific talent, commercial entrepreneurship, and military expertise that will be vital to an Academy experience for the talented individuals it will support and develop. We are confident that when given full and fair consideration, Maryland will stand out as the best and right choice for the United States Space Academy,” the members conclude. U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks and U.S. Representatives Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Glenn Ivey, Sarah Elfreth, April McClain Delaney, and Johnny Olszewski (all D-Md.) are pushing the Trump Administration for answers after finding significant increases in processing delays and denials of naturalization applications at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Baltimore Field Office. The lawmakers point to concerning trends they have encountered that have left those seeking citizenship in the lurch – from seeing USCIS decide significantly fewer cases, to witnessing process times doubling, to learning of the frequent cancellation of citizenship ceremonies. The Maryland delegation members urge USCIS Director Joseph Edlow to take immediate corrective action to address the discrepancies and stress the need for approved applicants to promptly be scheduled for the oath ceremonies they are eligible for under law. The lawmakers begin , “We write to raise serious concerns regarding the current state of the processing of naturalization applications (USCIS Form N-400, Application for Naturalization) pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services at the Baltimore Field Office.” “A recent review of USCIS’s quarterly data revealed that the agency has decided 73% fewer naturalization cases over the past year—the lowest level over the past decade. Press Unpause, a grassroots organization that closely tracked the impacts of these policies, estimated that over 2 million filed applications were subject to USCIS’s adjudicative hold over the almost 7 months that it was in place. That is 2 million people whose lives were put on hold, which led to compounding consequences across employment, finances, health, housing, family, and legal status for so many,” they continue . On the increased processing times in USCIS’ Baltimore Filed Office, the Maryland delegation members write , “These delays have disproportionately impacted Marylanders. Between June 1, 2026, and October 22, 2026, processing times for naturalization applications at USCIS’s Baltimore Field Office have nearly doubled: increasing from about 8 months to a year to a range of 15 to more than 20 months – more than a year and a half. The significant rise in average processing times for naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office is deeply concerning, especially when compared to other large USCIS Field Offices nationally. The Baltimore Field Office currently adjudicates naturalization applications slower than major Field Offices in New York City (10 to 12.5 months), Orlando (13.5 to 18.5 months), Miami (10 to 14.5 months), Dallas (13 to 16 months) and Los Angeles (10.5 to 14 months). Meanwhile, similar cases in the neighboring office in Washington, DC are adjudicated within a range of 11.5 to 14 months on average.” “Finally, the cancellation of oath ceremonies—the last step to becoming an American citizen, when individuals swear their loyalty to the United States and receive their Certificate of Naturalization—have caused significant delays for applicants who were vetted, received full approval, and passed their required citizenship exams. American citizenship bestows critical rights and responsibilities upon those who earn it, including the right to vote and the responsibility of serving as a juror in our justice system. Needless postponement unfairly withholds those important rights and responsibilities from those who have earned them,” the lawmakers note. “We urge USCIS to take immediate corrective action to address the extraordinary decline in the adjudication of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office, examine the alarming increase in denial rates, and ensure that approved applicants are promptly scheduled for oath ceremonies. We request a written response within 30 days outlining the specific steps USCIS is taking to restore timely adjudications, address the growing backlog, and establish a reasonable timeline for returning the Baltimore Field Office to normal processing operations. The thousands of Marylanders who have fulfilled their obligations under our immigration laws deserve more than indefinite delays. They deserve a fair, timely, and transparent path to citizenship. We expect USCIS to fulfill its responsibilities accordingly,” they conclude. The full text of the letter is available here and below. Dear Director Edlow: We write to raise serious concerns regarding the current state of the processing of naturalization applications (USCIS Form N-400, Application for Naturalization) pending with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services at the Baltimore Field Office. On June 5, 2026, a federal judge ruled that the policies set forth in U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ (USCIS) Policy Memorandum 602-0194, which halted the processing of key immigration benefit adjudications, were unlawful and vacated them nationwide. As a result, USCIS is legally obligated to resume standard processing of all applications that were previously paused and applications can no longer be arbitrarily held due to the applicant’s nationality. Despite vacating these policies, many naturalization applications continue to experience a substantial delay, with no information on a timeline for final adjudication or oath ceremony scheduling. Since the aforementioned ruling in Dorcas v. USCIS, our offices have received substantial outreach from constituents whose naturalization applications continue to be excessively stalled and subject to increasing processing times. A recent review of USCIS’s quarterly data revealed that the agency has decided 73% fewer naturalization cases over the past year—the lowest level over the past decade. Press Unpause, a grassroots organization that closely tracked the impacts of these policies, estimated that over 2 million filed applications were subject to USCIS’s adjudicative hold over the almost 7 months that it was in place. That is 2 million people whose lives were put on hold, which led to compounding consequences across employment, finances, health, housing, family, and legal status for so many. These delays have disproportionately impacted Marylanders. Between June 1, 2026, and October 22, 2026, processing times for naturalization applications at USCIS’s Baltimore Field Office have nearly doubled: increasing from about 8 months to a year to a range of 15 to more than 20 months – more than a year and a half. The significant rise in average processing times for naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office is deeply concerning, especially when compared to other large USCIS Field Offices nationally. The Baltimore Field Office currently adjudicates naturalization applications slower than major Field Offices in New York City (10 to 12.5 months), Orlando (13.5 to 18.5 months), Miami (10 to 14.5 months), Dallas (13 to 16 months) and Los Angeles (10.5 to 14 months). Meanwhile, similar cases in the neighboring office in Washington, DC are adjudicated within a range of 11.5 to 14 months on average. Also concerning are the drastic changes in adjudication rates and decisions. As of September 8, 2026, USCIS quarterly data from Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) reflected that the denial rate of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office increased fivefold: rising from 7% in the second quarter (Q2) to 35% in the third quarter (Q3). This means that more than one in three applications adjudicated during this quarter was denied, compared to less than one in ten previously. It’s also a roughly sixfold increase over naturalization application denial rates in the previous fiscal year (FY25). Further, the Baltimore Field Office adjudicated only 391 naturalization applications in Q3, compared with 1,178 in Q2 which is a 67% decrease from an already low level. This amounts to only five adjudications per business day, approximately. In direct comparison to previous years, during Q2 of FY25, 5,758 applications were adjudicated, while in Q3, 5,433 applications were adjudicated. This reflects an 80% and 93% decrease, respectively, in comparable quarters from FY25 to FY26. There are now nearly 17,000 Marylanders awaiting decisions on their naturalization applications. Finally, the cancellation of oath ceremonies—the last step to becoming an American citizen, when individuals swear their loyalty to the United States and receive their Certificate of Naturalization—have caused significant delays for applicants who were vetted, received full approval, and passed their required citizenship exams. American citizenship bestows critical rights and responsibilities upon those who earn it, including the right to vote and the responsibility of serving as a juror in our justice system. Needless postponement unfairly withholds those important rights and responsibilities from those who have earned them. As a nation of immigrants, we believe that individuals who navigate our legal immigration system in good faith deserve timely processing of their applications. A prolonged backlog of naturalization applications after a federal court directed USCIS to resume standard processing of these applications undermines the rule of law and the integrity of our country’s legal immigration system. We urge USCIS to take immediate corrective action to address the extraordinary decline in the adjudication of naturalization applications at the Baltimore Field Office, examine the alarming increase in denial rates, and ensure that approved applicants are promptly scheduled for oath ceremonies. We request a written response within 30 days outlining the specific steps USCIS is taking to restore timely adjudications, address the growing backlog, and establish a reasonable timeline for returning the Baltimore Field Office to normal processing operations. The thousands of Marylanders who have fulfilled their obligations under our immigration laws deserve more than indefinite delays. They deserve a fair, timely, and transparent path to citizenship. We expect USCIS to fulfill its responsibilities accordingly.

Today, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), along with more than ten of his colleagues, is pressing Senate and House leadership to exclude provisions in the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) that would require the President to expand and enhance defense cooperation and intelligence sharing with the Government of Israel. These provisions would undermine the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests at a time when the Government of Israel’s actions are increasingly not aligned with those interests. This effort follows a Dear Colleague letter sent by Senator Van Hollen in July urging Senators to oppose any motion to proceed on the NDAA vote until these provisions were addressed. Senator Van Hollen was joined in sending this letter by Senators Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Elizabeth Warren, (D-Mass.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and Andy Kim (D-N.J.). U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is pressing the Trump Administration for accountability following the death of Maryland resident Julian Curo-Churata in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody and subsequent apparent retaliation against Mr. Curo-Churata’s wife. U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Committee, wrote to Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chair Paul Atkins with concerns that a recent slate of deregulatory proposals purportedly aimed at “making IPOs great again” would reduce transparency, damage investor confidence, and undermine the integrity of America’s capital markets. In May, Chair Atkins announced an effort to “Make IPOs Great Again” and encourage more companies to “go and stay public.” While the policy initiative aims to reverse the decline in publicly-listed U.S. companies over the past three decades by reducing public-market disclosures and requirements, research shows that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason why fewer companies have gone public. The Senators note that the SEC’s proposals would be counterproductive and risk exacerbating the decline in public companies. “While we share the goal of revitalizing the public markets and providing more companies with the opportunity to go public, the ill-conceived deregulatory measures you have taken will not revive or sustain a healthy IPO market,” wrote the Senators . “These proposals would ultimately erode the very framework of transparency and investor protections that makes our public markets so appealing to investors the world over.” “Your proposals posit that the compliance burden of the robust regulations and disclosures required in the public markets is the sole reason that companies choose to stay private,” the Senators continued . “Academic research has repeatedly discredited your theory and found that more – not less – disclosure from public companies can make markets more liquid, is rewarded by investors with greater returns, and associated with larger stock markets. Moreover, research has shown that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason for why companies do not go public.” “Our capital markets thrive when more companies go public and go public earlier. Transparency and robust disclosure in our public markets facilitates a more trustworthy and efficient market where Main Street investors are more willing to provide capital because they have faith in the integrity of public markets,” wrote the Senators . “Our goal should be bringing as much capital raising as possible into our public markets to provide more growth opportunities for American companies and more wealth-building opportunities for the broadest range of American investors.” “As the SEC guts regulations protecting investors from untested issuers, the Commission is simultaneously ‘reliev(ing) a significant portion of all publicly traded issuers from making a wide variety of disclosures that they are currently required to provide,’” the Senators continued . “The result of this wholesale rollback of required disclosure requirements would almost certainly increase the level of fraud and raise the cost of capital.” The Senators requested that the letter be added to the comment file for all four of the SEC’s proposed deregulatory rules. The full text of the letter is available here and below. Dear Chairman Atkins, We write to urge the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC,” or “the Commission”) to reconsider its recent slew of proposals to weaken or eliminate longstanding regulations governing publicly traded company disclosures that make American capital markets the envy of the world. Although you claim to want to “Make IPOs Great Again,” the SEC’s specific proposals to deregulate the public company registration and disclosure regime represent an unprecedented attack on investors’ rights to transparency from public companies and threaten to undermine investor protection and market integrity. Your broad deregulatory agenda would compromise the integrity of our capital markets at a moment when Americans are already reeling from spiraling costs and unprecedented corruption in the Trump economy. We urge you to rescind these recent proposals that would put families and investors at even greater risk. On May 19, you announced an initiative to “Make IPOs Great Again” intended to encourage more companies to “go and stay public.” This agenda purportedly aims to reverse the decline in the number of U.S. public listings over the last three decades, from a peak of over 8,000 in 1996 to roughly 4,000 in 2024. To that end, you promulgated two rulemakings that would allow more than 80% of public companies to provide less disclosure based on their size and would enable virtually any newly public company to immediately raise more capital with “short-form” registration statements previously reserved for large, seasoned companies. While we share the goal of revitalizing the public markets and providing more companies with the opportunity to go public, the ill-conceived deregulatory measures you have taken will not revive or sustain a healthy IPO market. Instead, the flawed rationale that requiring less disclosure from public companies will motivate more companies to conduct IPOs has been repeatedly debunked. These proposals would ultimately erode the very framework of transparency and investor protections that makes our public markets so appealing to investors the world over. What’s more, the proposals misconstrue the actual root causes of the decline in the IPO market and do nothing to address the real issue: weak regulation in private markets that incentivizes companies to stay private. Requiring less disclosure from public companies will only damage investor confidence and undermine the integrity of American public markets. Data Suggests Deregulatory Measures Do Not Result in Increased IPOs. The Real Problem is Underregulated Private Markets. Your proposals posit that the compliance burden of the robust regulations and disclosures required in the public markets is the sole reason that companies choose to stay private. Academic research has repeatedly discredited your theory and found that more – not less – disclosure from public companies can make markets more liquid, is rewarded by investors with greater returns, and associated with larger stock markets. Moreover, research has shown that deregulation in the private markets is a key reason for why companies do not go public. One study shows that Sarbanes-Oxley-era regulations, for example, which increased corporate financial reporting rules and internal controls for public companies, were not the core cause of the declining IPOs after the law’s adoption in the early 2000s. Instead, declines in IPOs were attributed to a changing market environment in which smaller companies had greater profit potential through acquisition channels, not IPOs. Another study attributes the IPO decline to major private market deregulation in the years prior to Sarbanes-Oxley. The reforms expanded the number of investors permitted in private funds that are not subject to comprehensive SEC oversight, among other deregulatory measures such as preempting state regulation of certain private offerings. These reforms ballooned the supply of private capital available to private companies which significantly contributed to companies opting to stay private entirely or stay private for longer. Expanded opportunities to raise capital with less expense and oversight in the private markets has created a structural disincentive to going public. In other words, it is not that public markets are overregulated, it is that private markets are underregulated, and repeated deregulatory reforms have pulled more and more capital from the public markets into the private markets. Lighter regulatory requirements – such as no obligation to provide investors with financial statements, quarterly reports, material event reporting, or disclosure about executive compensation – have incentivized a growing number of companies to raise capital in the private markets rather than go public. For example, the number of offerings under Regulation D – which provides the most commonly used exemptions from SEC registration requirements allowing companies to raise money without going public – have increased by more than 150% over the last 16 years. In 2009, there were nearly 14,000 offerings and $588 billion in capital raised through Reg D. In 2025, there were more than 34,000 offerings raising nearly $2.4 trillion. And yet, under your leadership, the SEC is not only failing to strengthen guardrails in private markets, it is proposing to dramatically weaken guardrails in public markets. Like other similar deregulatory efforts in the past, your proposals are unlikely to achieve their stated goal of incentivizing capital raising in our public markets by lowering the bar for transparency from public companies. Weakening regulations for public companies, for example, was the inspiration of the JOBS Act of 2012, which was designed to improve “access to the public capital markets for emerging growth companies” and “seeks to remove impediments for “emerging” public companies by relaxing disclosure, governance and accounting requirements, [and] easing the restrictions on analyst communications.” The bill also included provisions “designed to allow some private companies to defer going public, including provisions raising the threshold for registration under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.” However, the data since 2012 shows that this policy prescription did not consistently increase the number of public companies in the 14 years since. According to a University of Florida study, the market netted 158 new IPOs the year after the JOBS Act passed Congress. Last year, it netted only 90. There has not been a return to 1990’s IPO levels, where the lowest number of net new IPOs per year was 110, and the high was 677 new IPOs. History has already taught us that deregulation in the public markets does not result in major gains in IPOs over a long-time period. Our capital markets thrive when more companies go public and go public earlier. Transparency and robust disclosure in our public markets facilitates a more trustworthy and efficient market where Main Street investors are more willing to provide capital because they have faith in the integrity of public markets. Conversely, private markets are intentionally limited to a smaller population of highly sophisticated investors because their lack of transparency and regulation increases the risk of fraud and loss. Our goal should be bringing as much capital raising as possible into our public markets to provide more growth opportunities for American companies and more wealth-building opportunities for the broadest range of American investors. The SEC is Pushing to Deregulate Public Markets Anyway, Undermining Confidence in Our Markets and Leaving Investors in the Dark The data is clear that lowering the bar for public company disclosure is unlikely to significantly increase IPOs. Nevertheless, this SEC seems intent on destroying the most fundamental parts of our public company offering and reporting regime with the recent rule proposals discussed in detail below. a. Deregulating Registered Offerings In May, the SEC proposed a broad range of changes that upset the historical balance between investor protection and managing costs for companies. These include a number of changes to the Commission’s framework for regulating public offerings. The federal securities laws generally require that companies file lengthy registration statements that go through an in-depth review by SEC staff before a company is able to offer securities to the investing public. This statutory requirement applies to all companies – newly public companies and existing public companies looking to sell additional securities – to ensure investor protection and market integrity. However, the SEC offers some efficiencies to large, established companies with an SEC reporting history, a category called “Well-Known Seasoned Issuers” (“WKSIs”), on the theory that market participants already have sufficient information about these “established” companies to ensure market integrity and investor protection. One such benefit is the ability to use “Form S-3”, a “short form” registration statement that allows companies to (1) incorporate information from its other SEC filings and (2) to time their offerings based on market conditions. WKSIs also qualify to have these registration statements become effective automatically, without SEC staff review, providing flexibility with respect to offering timing. As a result, WKSIs have significant responsibility to be forthcoming and accurate. When the SEC does not review a registration statement in such circumstances, the Commission has less of an opportunity to ensure that disclosures are not misleading, that allowing a company to proceed with the offering is in the public interest, and that the offering is consistent with the protection of investors. WKSIs are also offered other special benefits, including the ability to be able to communicate with investors before a registration statement is filed with the SEC. This existing framework, which offers certain accommodations to large, established public companies, is premised on the market having sufficient information about the company such that the full registration process is not necessary to ensure investor protection. The SEC’s recent proposal would significantly expand the narrowly afforded exceptions to a much broader population of companies – effectively eliminating the concept of “WKSIs” altogether. Among other changes, the SEC’s proposed registered offering amendments remove key requirements to use Form S-3. The proposal lowers the issuer market cap size threshold, shortens the minimum period during which the company has to have been public, and removes the requirement that the issuer has made required dividend and debt payments. The rule, if implemented, would allow untested issuers, even those who have not complied with their financial obligations, to have instant access to the market without meaningful oversight by the SEC. The SEC is opening the floodgates to an “increase of over 60 percent in the number of issuers eligible” to use Form S-3. The SEC also proposes to eliminate the WKSIs’ market size framework and replace it with a different system of categorization that the SEC estimates would create a 200% increase in the number of issuers eligible for the benefits currently reserved for WKSIs, despite such issuers being neither “well-known” nor “seasoned.” This significant expansion to the WKSI definition is inconsistent with why the SEC created these efficiencies in the first place. Under your proposal, the WKSI exception becomes the rule. The proposed expansion to the WKSI definition would mean that only a minority of companies would be subject to the statutory requirement for full registration statement disclosure and staff review. The result is less seasoned companies are able to take investors’ money with less disclosure and less oversight from the SEC. In addition to expanding exemptions from the securities laws, the proposal also preempts state securities laws requiring registration for offerings of unlisted securities. Preemption of state registration hinders the ability of state law enforcement to protect investors from wrongdoers – especially as the SEC has had record-low levels of enforcement under your leadership. Under current law, non-listed companies that have not registered with the SEC may still be subject to state-level regulations to protect investors. The SEC’s proposed change would mean that investors in public, non-listed real estate investment trusts and business development companies will no longer have the protections of state registration and regulatory review. The proposed rule also offers registration and communication benefits to business development companies (“BDCs”) and closed-end funds. This loosening of rules for these investment vehicles comes just as BDCs and the related private-credit market experience significant market challenges. b. Deregulating Public Reporting As the SEC guts regulations protecting investors from untested issuers, the Commission is simultaneously “reliev[ing] a significant portion of all publicly traded issuers from making a wide variety of disclosures that they are currently required to provide.” The result of this wholesale rollback of required disclosure requirements would almost certainly increase the level of fraud and raise the cost of capital. Under the proposal, accommodations created for smaller reporting companies and emerging growth companies are extended to many more companies — including large issuers with significant market impact. These accommodations result in reduced disclosures on executive compensation, fewer years of audited financials, and eliminating the “say-on-pay” requirement for investors to vote on executive compensation. Eliminating requirements on executive compensation, as required by Dodd-Frank following the Great Recession, appears to be a signature move by the Trump Administration to insulate corporate executives from any accountability or reasonable governance. The proposal also raises the threshold for qualifying for strict reporting deadlines applicable to the largest companies, making it so fewer companies have to get information to investors expeditiously at the end of a given quarter. Additionally, the proposed rules increase the number of companies that would no longer be required to have auditors reviewing and attesting to their internal controls. Auditors serve as a critical gatekeeper to ensuring that internal controls exist to ensure reliability and accuracy of companies’ financial reports. This deregulatory rule does little to shift the balance of incentives away from raising capital from private capital markets; and only worsens the quality of information and governance in our public markets. c. Other Deregulatory Proposals The Commission is also advancing several other deregulatory proposals that amount to an overhaul of longstanding SEC policies meant to protect investors and ensure market integrity. First, the SEC is allowing public companies to report their earnings to investors less frequently. Since 1970, public companies have been required to report quarterly earnings to investors on Form 10-Q. The SEC’s proposal would upend over half a century of standard practice by allowing companies to report their earnings only semiannually, on a new Form 10-S. As some experts have argued, “U.S. capital markets have remained liquid and robust due in part to investor confidence in the quality and frequency of the information released by companies. A reduction in the frequency of mandatory reporting could result in reduced information flow to investors and less analyst coverage, hampering investors’ ability to make informed decisions, with potentially adverse consequences for the smooth operation of the markets.” Recognizing these concerns, the public has flooded the SEC with a record over 200,000 comment letters, 99 percent of which oppose the rule. Additionally, the SEC has proposed rescinding the rule it adopted in 2024 requiring public companies to disclose climate-related risks to investors. First proposed in 2022, this rule would have required companies to include in their prospectuses “information about climate-related risks that are reasonably likely to have a material impact on their business, results of operations, or financial condition, and certain climate-related financial statement metrics in a note to their audited financial statements.” Walking back this rule will leave investors with less information about risks to their investment, threatening their ability to make informed decisions and enhance market liquidity. Senator Whitehouse and I sent a letter to the SEC on August 3, 2026, asking the SEC to reconsider the proposed rescission of the climate-risk disclosure rule. Conclusion Taken together, your “making IPOs great again” agenda is part and parcel of the Trump Administration’s approach to our financial markets: make it easier for the President’s billionaire donors and corporate executives to avoid accountability or transparency, while leaving regular investors in the dark. Not only will this undermine the reputation of our markets as the most transparent and liquid in the world, but it will also likely fail at its stated goal of actually increasing the number of IPOs and put American investors at greater risk of being defrauded. These proposals should be reconsidered so that the United States public markets can remain the world’s gold standard. I request that this letter be added to the file for the following rules: ? U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) joined Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on the Census, led a bipartisan group of 24 colleagues urging the U.S. Census Bureau to rescind a proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from census counts and eliminate questions on race and ethnicity. In their letter, the Senators warn that the exclusion of non-citizens violates the Constitution, which expressly says that the census must count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The Bureau has proposed two methods by which it would exclude non-citizens, both of which would cause undercounts and errors in the census counts. “We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain non-citizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census. The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the ‘whole number of persons in each state.’ The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services,” the senators wrote. The letter also describes how the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions would undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws and would degrade the quality of all census data. The compliance of civil and voting rights laws rely on demographic data, and only the decennial census provides accurate and precise data. Additionally, eliminating the collection of race and ethnicity data from the decennial census undermines other federal survey data. Businesses and local governments that depend on such data have said that they would be harmed by this proposed rule. “In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule ‘deteriorates the accuracy’ of ‘fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation’ because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates,” the senators continued. “The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded.” Joining Senators Peters and Kim in sending the letter were Senators Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Angus King (I-Maine), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.). The full text of the letter is available here and below. Dear Under Secretary Meyer and Deputy Under Secretary Cook, We write to urge that you rescind your proposed rule that would exclude certain noncitizens from decennial census counts and omit questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census (Fed. Reg. Vol. 91, No. 57524, Thursday September 10, 2026). The proposed rule violates the clear meaning of the Constitution, which requires that the Census Bureau count the “whole number of persons in each state.” The proposed rule would also cause communities across the country to be counted inaccurately, jeopardizing their fair representation in Congress and access to billions of federal dollars for education, health care, and public safety services. The proposed rule would also undermine the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws by eliminating the only appropriate data used for compliance. We request that you rescind this proposed rule to ensure the decennial census complies with the Constitution and allows civil and voting rights laws to be enforced. I. The Bureau’s Proposal to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens from Census Counts Violates the Constitution The proposal to exclude certain non-citizens, including those who are legal immigrants, from apportionment counts violates the Constitution. The Fourteenth Amendment is clear: the Census Bureau must count the “whole number of persons in each state” in the United States, including non-citizens. This interpretation of the Constitution has been accepted from the founding of our nation to the present, by our founders, courts, members of Congress, and leaders of the Census Bureau from both parties, including Secretary Howard Lutnick. In 1788, James Madison wrote in Federalist No. 54 that the apportionment was to be “founded on the aggregate number of inhabitants,” recognizing no distinctions among types of persons to be counted except for those explicitly excluded in the text of the Constitution itself. During consideration of the Fourteenth Amendment, Congress debated and expressly rejected proposals to change the “persons” counted for apportionment to “voters” or “citizens.” During the first half of the twentieth century, Congress considered and rejected proposals to pass statutes to exclude non-citizens from apportionment counts on the basis that it would take a constitutional amendment to change the requirement. In 1929, the Senate’s Legislative Counsel concluded that excluding certain noncitizens from apportionment counts would be unconstitutional. In 1980, a court rejected a lawsuit seeking that the Bureau exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. Even current Secretary of Commerce Lutnick testified to Congress in February that “citizenship is not in the Constitution for the [Census] apportionment... that is not a necessary factor”. This unbroken history of our reading of the Constitution, including courts, Congress, and Census Bureau leaders, is clear: the Census Bureau must count every person. II. The Bureau’s Proposed Methods to Exclude Certain Non-Citizens Would Cause Undercounts and Errors in Census Counts The Bureau has proposed two methods for carrying out its unconstitutional exclusion of certain non-citizens: directly asking every person detailed questions about their immigration status and relying on administrative records. Both proposed methods would cause undercounts of both citizens and non-citizens and errors in the population counts. First, the Bureau proposes asking each person their legal immigration status so that it can exclude certain non-citizens, but such a question would cause both citizens and non-citizens to not answer the census. This would likely lead to undercounts and errors in census counts. The Bureau has never asked detailed questions about legal immigration status on any nationwide survey before, let alone the decennial census, because of concerns about privacy and accuracy. The Bureau’s own research before the 2020 Census showed that including even a question about citizenship status on the decennial census, itself a less complicated question than immigration status, would cause fewer citizens and non-citizens to complete the census. In addition, the Government Accountability Office previously found that if statistical agencies directly asked about immigration status, they would create invalid, imprecise, and inaccurate estimates. In 2006, the Government Accountability Office recommended that federal agencies should not pursue adding even indirect immigration questions to surveys, and the Census Bureau concurred with that recommendation. In addition, the Bureau alternatively proposes relying on administrative records acquired from federal agencies, state and local governments, and private data brokers to exclude certain non-citizens from apportionment counts. This approach would also lead to undercounts and inappropriately exclude citizens and non-citizens from census totals. The Bureau previously found that if it relied solely on administrative records the decennial census would misestimate the total population by over 1.3 million people, overcounting non-citizens and undercounting citizens. It also found that relying on administrative records undercounted people in rural areas and group quarters, such as nursing homes and college campuses. The Treasury Department commented on a draft of this very rule warning that using tax records to identify people’s usual address would cause people to be counted in the wrong location. This evidence shows that both of the Bureau’s proposed methods to carry out this unconstitutional effort would cause errors and undercounts, denying people fair representation in Congress and jeopardizing the fair and full allocation of resources. III. The Bureau’s Proposal to Omit Demographic Questions Would Undermine Enforcement of Civil and Voting Rights Laws and Degrade the Quality of All Census Data We also express our strong opposition to the Bureau’s proposal to eliminate race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census, because it would harm the ability to enforce civil and voting rights laws and cause the quality of all census data to deteriorate. Only the decennial census provides the reliable demographic data necessary for compliance with civil and voting rights laws. Congress has made clear that decennial census data should be used to enforce these laws, and the Trump Administration even recognized the legal need to collect this data for enforcing civil rights laws when it published its planned questions for the 2020 Census. For example, Congress enacted the Fair Housing Act, the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Public Health Service Act to ensure that individuals are not discriminated against on the basis of race or ethnicity in housing, employment, and health care, respectively. The Supreme Court has held that statistical evidence using census data can be used to demonstrate violations and ensure compliance with these laws. The Bureau admits in its own regulatory filing that no other federal survey that collects information about race and ethnicity, including the American Community Survey (ACS), can substitute for the decennial census, because other surveys like the ACS cannot create precise population estimates for areas smaller than 65,000 people. This means there is no real alternative for all Americans to bring claims under civil rights laws if the Bureau eliminates collecting information about race and ethnicity on the decennial census. Similarly, Congress enacted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to prohibit voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race, including congressional redistricting. While the Supreme Court narrowed the standards to bring a claim under the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais, the Court maintained that the Voting Rights Act is violated “when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race.” Such evidence requires the availability of decennial census data about race and ethnicity for enforcement, because the Voting Rights Act applies to even small political subdivisions where no other federal data is accurate. The elimination of data about race and ethnicity would particularly undermine the federal government’s ability to meet its responsibilities and obligations to tribal governments. By eliminating the collection of information about American Indian and Alaska Native identity, the Bureau makes it effectively impossible for the government to administer the Indian Housing Block Grant program, the Indian Community Development Block Grant program, and the Indian Health Service – each of which depend on accurate estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations to plan and allocate funding. In its own regulatory filing, the Bureau admits that other federal surveys “may not be a suitable substitute for all federally recognized tribes,” because other surveys do not provide accurate and precise estimates of American Indian and Alaska Native populations. The Bureau previously told Congress that relying on alternative options to collect information about American Indian and Alaska Native populations, like asking about tribal enrollment or relying on administrative records, would cause inaccurate estimates and infringe on the private sovereign information of tribes. In its attempt to undermine the data used for the enforcement of civil and voting rights laws, the Bureau will degrade the accuracy of all other federal survey data, particularly for small and rural geographic areas. The Bureau writes in its own regulatory filing that the proposed rule "deteriorates the accuracy” of “fertility/mortality rates, cancer rates, poverty rates, unemployment rates, [and] labor force participation” because the Bureau relies on accurate decennial census information to adjust and design other survey estimates. The Bureau also admits in its filing that the proposal would hamper the usability of data for state and local governments who rely on precise and accurate population estimates for small geographic areas. Businesses and local governments that depend on reliable and complete federal data have warned that the Census Bureau’s proposal would increase costs as data is degraded. With these considerations in mind, we urge the Census Bureau to rescind its September 10 proposed regulation. Sincerely,

Today, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) joined Representative Scott Peters (D-Calif.-50) and over 60 bicameral Members of Congress on a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, demanding the immediate cancellation of any deportation flights carrying Afghans and Iranians, whether sent directly or through another country. This letter comes after reports that over 150 Afghans could be deported to Pakistan in the coming days, which would constitute one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans ever . San Diego has served as a primary hub for incoming Afghan refugees, with nearly 5,000 resettling in the region. The Members also expressed concern over another flight with a mass deportation of Iranians — the first since the U.S. launched its military conflict against Iran— and that relatives of Afghans who helped American troops could be among those on board. “Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families’ safety to stand by U.S. service members,” the Members wrote, adding that deporting them “is a violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops.” The Members emphasized the well-documented danger awaiting deportees. The State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” country, and for those who aided U.S. forces, “their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day.” They detail the torture, detention, and extrajudicial killing of dissidents and LGBTQ persons, as well as the severe repression of women — noting that women and LGBTQ refugees could be on the flight. The Members also raised alarm over reports that Iranians, including women, Christian converts, and pro-democracy activists, may be deported to Iran, where they face imprisonment, torture, and a possible death sentence. “Sending people who sought protection from the Islamic Republic of Iran back to a war zone and a repressive regime is unconscionable,” they wrote. They cited how even President Trump has warned about the dangers faced by pro-democracy and anti-government protesters in Iran. The Members stressed that routing a flight through a third country does not change U.S. obligations, and urged the Trump Administration to warn Pakistan that the U.S. will not accept its participation in sending deportees onward to the Taliban. These individuals “came to the U.S. because they believed in its promise of democracy, religious freedom, and liberty,” the Members concluded, and “we must uphold those values and commitments, not abandon people to autocratic regimes.” “Sixty-six members of Congress, from both chambers, needed less than 24 hours to say what every veteran of the Afghanistan war already knows: you don’t hand the people who stood with our troops to the Taliban. When even the Taliban are voicing ‘serious concern’ about your deportation plan, you’ve lost the moral argument and the national security one. This flight isn’t immigration enforcement. It’s a betrayal with a boarding pass, and the whole world is watching whether America keeps its word. We are grateful to Rep. Peters for leading. Secretary Rubio and Secretary Mullin, ground this plane,” said Shawn VanDiver, U.S. Navy veteran and President and Founder of #AfghanEvac. "Having effectively dismantled our protection system, this administration is set to deport vulnerable people back to Afghanistan and Iran, in violation of our human rights commitments and our nation's values," said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. "So many of these men and women never had a meaningful opportunity to defend their claims and are now the casualties of this administration's assault on asylum. We thank Congressman Peters for his leadership and all the members standing against these unconscionable deportations back to persecution, torture, or even death." The Members requested an immediate response. The full text of the letter is available here and below. Dear Secretary Rubio and Secretary Mullin, We are writing about the alarming reports that over 150 Afghans could be deported to Afghanistan in the coming days. This flight has now been reported in multiple court filings and media outlets, and as the New York Times notes, it would constitute “one of the largest single expulsions of Afghans” ever. We understand that relatives of Afghans who helped our troops could be on this flight. We have also received credible reports that this flight will be followed by the first mass deportation of Iranians since the United States launched its military conflict against Iran. We are extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people who sought safety in the United States to Afghanistan or Iran will result in their persecution, torture, or even death. We urge you to cancel any deportation flights of Afghans and Iranians, either directly or through any other country. Our nation made a promise to stand by Afghans who risked their lives and their families’ safety to stand by U.S. service members. This mass deportation – potentially to their deaths – is a violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops. As you know, Afghanistan remains an extremely dangerous country, and particularly deadly for the people who supported the U.S. government and troops. The U.S. State Department lists Afghanistan as a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” list and where many of those on the flight are likely to be persecuted, tortured, or even killed. Afghans who helped U.S. forces and who were left during the speedy evacuation have gone into hiding, been targeted for persecution and in some cases killed. Their assistance to U.S. troops puts a target on these individuals and their families to this day. Dissidents, LGBTQ persons, and many others who do not “conform” to the Taliban’s extremely restrictive rules have been subject to torture, detention, and extrajudicial killings. For women, Afghanistan is the most repressive country in the world; not only are girls and women excluded from education and public life, but many have been detained and beaten by authorities for “morality crimes.” Women have been subjected to rape and other sexual violence by the Taliban and other authorities, including as punishment for exercising their rights to press speech or as “discipline” by a husband. LGBTQ people in Afghanistan, where their status is largely criminalized, are routinely targeted for abuse and sexual violence, and their families are also targeted and persecuted by the Taliban. We have heard that there could be women and LGBTQ persons on this flight; if they are deported to Afghanistan, they will face extreme danger. We are similarly shocked to receive reports that this administration may also deport several Iranians – including women, Christian converts, and pro-democracy activists – to Iran, where they face imprisonment, torture, and in some cases, a possible death sentence. The United States has not ceased its military operations against Iran, and sending people who sought protection from the Islamic Republic of Iran back to a war zone and a repressive regime is unconscionable. In the U.S. State Department’s last human rights report on Iran, in 2024, it recorded: “The government executed hundreds of prisoners, including many who confessed under torture and faced unfair trials. There were new cases of violent enforcement of women’s dress code restrictions. While some political prisoners, including persons detained in connection with protests related to the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, were released from prison, other participants in the protests were arrested, sentenced to prison and death, subjected to torture, or executed during the year. Restrictions on religious freedom were severe during the year. ” President Trump has himself warned about the dangers faced by pro-democracy and anti-government protestors, including women, in Iran, and sending these individuals to Iran would expose them to significant harm. Sending dozens of people back to one of the most dangerous countries on earth, and where they are likely to be targeted for their or their family’s suspected support of the U.S. government or criticism of the Taliban, is a death sentence. Our country made a promise never to abandon the Afghans who sacrificed their own and their family’s safety to stand with American service members. The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way. It is the policy of the United States not to effect the involuntary return of any person to a country where there are substantial grounds for believing they would be in danger of being subjected to torture. The New York Times has reported that the plan is to fly Afghans from Louisiana to Pakistan. We also urge you to make clear to the Government of Pakistan that the United States will not accept its participation in sending these individuals onward to the Taliban. Under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act and Executive Order 13818, the United States may impose sanctions on foreign persons who are responsible for, complicit in, or materially assist serious human rights abuse. Officials who help deliver people to torture or death should expect us to press for exactly those sanctions, and for a full accounting of their role. We urge your agencies to cancel any plans for deportation flights to Iran or Afghanistan so that this administration is not complicit in horrendous human rights abuses. These people came to the U.S. because they believed in its promise of democracy, religious freedom, and liberty. We must uphold those values and commitments, not abandon people to autocratic regimes. We request a response to this letter by November 2nd and expect your assurances that these flights will not proceed. Sincerely,

As the American people increasingly worry about corporations and billionaire donors pumping millions of dollars into elections, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Congressman Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, are announcing new legislation to close the loophole that allows donors benefitting from federal contracts to pour increasingly obscene amounts of campaign contributions into American elections. The lawmakers’ bill would end the “Musk loophole” by expanding current law that prevents federal contractors from donating to a political party, candidate, or committee to ensure that those with the most to benefit – like corporate executives and major shareholders – fall within the law. “We need to end the rotten political system that allows individuals like Elon Musk to spend unlimited sums of money to elect candidates who turn around and vote to send your tax dollars to their corporations through huge federal contracts. This legislation will close that corrupt campaign cash-for-contracts loophole. It will help ensure that our federal government prioritizes the needs of the American people, not corporations making billions of dollars from taxpayer-funded federal contracts,” said Senator Van Hollen . “Federal contractors shouldn’t be able to use their positions to buy influence. This bill strengthens the ban on campaign contributions from senior federal contractors, ensuring that government contracts are awarded on merit, not political connections. I am proud to join Senator Van Hollen to hold federal contractors to the highest standards of accountability,” said Congressman Garcia . The legislation is supported by Campaign Legal Center, Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy 21, Public Citizen, End Citizens United Action Fund, Common Cause, Indivisible, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), Democracy Defenders Action, and Stand Up America. Americans across the country are watching in horror as billionaires and corporations attempt to influence our election system. For example, Elon Musk’s companies have received tens of billions of dollars in contracts from the federal government. At the same time, Musk donated over $290 million to President Trump and his Republican allies’ campaigns in the 2024 cycle and has spent a record-breaking more than $440 million in the 2026 cycle to help the Republican Party retain control of Congress. He is not the only one – many other individuals who control companies that benefit from federal contracts donate exorbitant sums of money to candidates and the PACs and Super PACs that help elect them. This legislation would expand current law – that has already been upheld by our court system – to put an end to that corruption. The Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act would: Expand the current ban to cover federal contractors’ executive office holders, major shareholders, and affiliated corporations Establish a one-year “cooling off” period after the completion of a federal contract to prohibit federal contractors from making contributions soon after finishing performance on a contract only then to seek additional contracts Prevent dark money organizations from being used as pass-throughs by requiring any federal contractor donations to be held separately and prohibit them from being spent on any campaigns or electoral materials Add a prohibition on accepting (as opposed to just soliciting) illegal federal contractor contributions Require illegal contributions to be turned over to the Treasury rather than simply refunded to the donor “For more than 75 years, federal law has barred government contractors from making political contributions to prevent lucrative, taxpayer-funded contracts from being sold to big donors,” said Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at Campaign Legal Center . “The idea of companies buying influence with the elected officials who help decide how to award federal contracts is such a clear avenue for corruption that courts have long upheld this law as an important tool for protecting voters. Unfortunately, federal contractors routinely exploit well-recognized gaps in the law to engage in the very pay-to-play corruption Congress intended to foreclose. That’s why Campaign Legal Center endorses the Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act. This important legislation will prevent corporate executives from circumventing this important prohibition, address the problem of contractors funneling illegal contributions through dark money groups, and ensure that the money contractors use to make illegal contributions is returned to taxpayers. We applaud Senator Van Hollen and Representative Garcia for introducing this bill and call on Congress to pass it without delay.” “Americans are furious about political corruption. Meanwhile, weak rules allow companies and individuals making huge profits from federal contracts to spend lavishly to help elect the very officials who influence how those contracts are awarded,” said Daniel Weiner, Senior Director of the Elections & Government Program at the Brennan Center for Justice . “That has to change. The Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act is a clear and necessary step to curb pay-for-play corruption and ensure Americans can have confidence that their money is spent wisely and their government is working for them.” “Democracy 21 strongly supports the Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act being introduced by Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representative Robert Garcia. This bill will close a massive loophole in the government contractor ban by extending its coverage to include contractors’ executive office holders, major shareholders, and affiliated corporations. You have to go no further than Elon Musk to understand why this new anti-corruption legislation is essential to protect the interests of the American people. Musk is the biggest campaign contributor in American history and his companies have many billions of dollars in government contracts. Musk is the poster child for why pay-to-play legislation must cover executive office holders and major shareholders if it is to accomplish its goals. We strongly commend Senator Van Hollen and Rep. Garcia for their leadership on this key government integrity legislation,” said Fred Wertheimer, President of Democracy 21 . “The Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act would put the brakes on wealthy special interests buying lucrative federal contracts through campaign donations. Wealthy entities all too often secure government contracts by making sizable campaign contributions to those responsible for awarding the contracts. Though federal law currently prohibits the actual ‘contracting entity’ from making such contributions, all the senior executives and owners get around the law by pooling individual contributions in the name of the contracting entity. Sen. Van Hollen's and Rep. Garcia's bill would close this loophole by simply extending the ban to the senior executives and owners of a contracting entity as well as the entity itself. Public Citizen heartily endorses this measure,” said Craig Holman, Ph.D., Public Citizen . “The current ban on federal contractors making political contributions is riddled with loopholes,” said End Citizens United Action Fund President Tiffany Muller . “Billionaires like Elon Musk are still able to pour hundreds of millions into our elections while their companies collect billions in government contracts. The Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act would prevent this pay-to-play corruption by extending the ban to executives, major shareholders, and affiliated companies. We thank Senator Van Hollen and Representative Garcia for their ongoing leadership in making sure taxpayer dollars are not used to reward political donors.” “Poll after poll shows that Americans are deeply concerned about corruption and want serious solutions to protect taxpayer dollars,” said Abigail Bellows, Senior Policy Director of Anti-corruption and Accountability at Common Cause . “That's why we applaud the introduction of the Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act. This bill would make it illegal for the people who benefit from federal contracts to pay off the very same politicians who decide where federal contracts go. Congress should pass this bill in order to make sure our tax dollars are spent responsibly – not steered toward politically connected contractors.” “Right now, millionaires and billionaires who own or control companies that contract with the federal government can evade protections meant to prevent federal contractors from engaging in pay-to-play schemes,” said Debra Perlin, Vice President for Policy at CREW . “The Close Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act would fix a gap in the law that allows executives, major shareholders and corporations affiliated with federal contractors to make contributions to political parties and candidates in an effort to gain an unfair advantage in securing or maintaining federal contracts. CREW is proud to endorse this legislation, sponsored by Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representative Robert Garcia, and urges Congress to act on it without delay.” “Americans deserve to know that their hard-earned tax dollars are spent wisely by public officials. If big government contractors are able to make large political contributions and get billions of dollars in contracts in return, this pay-to-play system shows that government is open to the highest bidder rather than the best value for the American people,” said Virginia Canter, Chief Counsel and Director of Anti-Corruption and Ethics at Democracy Defenders Action . “We applaud Senator Van Hollen and Ranking Member Garcia for their leadership for announcing the Close the Campaign Cash-for-Contracts Loophole Act. Today, U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) are calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to answer questions on the temporary removal of the No Kings Coalition Instagram account in the middle of nationwide demonstrations organized by the group. The No Kings Day account was shut down and organizers were unable to access it as nearly three thousand events were held across the country where Americans expressed their support for democracy, the right to vote, and democratic institutions. The lawmakers begin , “We are writing to seek answers regarding the removal of the No Kings Coalition Instagram account in the middle of nationwide protest demonstrations organized by the group. On October 17, 2026, Americans from all around the country gathered together in political demonstrations expressing support for democracy, the right to vote, and our democratic institutions organized by the No Kings Coalition. The No Kings Coalition uses Instagram as one of their primary platforms for communicating with participants, the public, and for hosting livestreams of their events. During the middle of these nationwide demonstrations, the No Kings Coalition’s Instagram account was mysteriously made invisible to the public, and the administrators were not able to access their account. The shutdown of the public page lasted well over an hour. Making matters worse, the lockout that prevented the account holders from even accessing their own page stretched for hours after the public page was restored, restricting their ability to communicate with supporters and protesters during the demonstrations despite the page being live.” “We are especially troubled by Meta’s changing explanation for removing the account’s public visibility and the organizers' access during a nationally attended and well-publicized event. Andy Stone, Vice President of Communications at Meta, first shared that the account was shut down because very high frequencies of posting, sharing, or commenting triggered automated systems. The next day, Mr. Stone claimed that it had nothing to do with the account’s posting, sharing, or commenting but on their ‘reading’ behavior and the rate at which they were ‘reading profiles, posts, and hashtags’ on October 17. He also recognized that it ‘took additional time for [Meta] to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account.’ Not only are Meta’s shifting explanations alarming, the substance of the claims paint the picture that one of the largest social media companies in the world is somehow incapable of handling technical concerns about an account without shutting it down for hours,” they continue . Noting that this is not an isolated incident, the lawmakers note , “This is not the first time that Meta has experienced shutdowns or lapses around political speech leading up to the 2026 elections. In September, Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown shared that a technical glitch with Facebook’s advertising platform caused about half of his campaign advertisements on the platform to be taken down for over a day without notice. Additionally, in Brazil, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was unable to boost his Instagram posts for almost 24 hours, while his opponent, who is known to be connected with the Trump Administration, was able to boost posts during the same time span.” “Furthermore, at a time when billionaires and big business, including Meta, are cozying up to the Trump Administration, we cannot ignore that it was a grassroots organization that is standing up to President Trump’s corruption that experienced this blackout. Meta’s close relationship with the Trump Administration is well documented. The company donated one million dollars to an inauguration fund for President Trump and five million dollars for Trump’s ballroom project. In settling a lawsuit, Meta also agreed to pay President Trump $25 million. The relationship between the Trump Administration, big business, and the media that these businesses run raises serious concerns over freedom of speech and the press,” the lawmakers conclude .
